summary: Suggests additions to the Internet mail format of RFC 822 for a Content-Type header field, so that messages can say what kind of content they carry. It was a proposal for discussion and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC asks Internet mail to carry a header field that says what kind of content a message body holds, so that a reading program can display it correctly. The body stays plain ASCII, and the memo asks for comments rather than setting a standard.

questions: what is the content-type header field
how did email first describe content types

subtitle: A proposed mail header that tells a reading program what kind of content a message body really holds.

tldr.problem: Mail bodies were plain ASCII strings, so a reader had no way to know that the text was really a formatted document that needed special processing to display correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a Content-Type header field with up to four parameters: a type naming the structuring technique, an optional version number, a resource reference, and a comment, with the body still limited to the ASCII characters allowed by RFC 822.
tldr.outcome: The memo asks for discussion rather than setting a standard, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it.

facts.label: Type values
facts.value: POSTSCRIPT, SCRIBE, SGML, TEX, TROFF, DVI, plus private X- values

facts.label: TROFF resource references
facts.value: eqn, tbl, me, or a local part

facts.label: Registration
facts.value: With the Internet Assigned Numbers Coordinator at USC-ISI

today: RFC 1049 is a March 1988 proposal for a Content-Type header field that asked for discussion and suggestions for improvement, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of that proposal.

sections.title: Why Mail Needed a Content Type
sections.content:
As defined in RFC 822, an electronic mail message consists of a number of defined header fields, some containing structured information such as date and addresses, and a message body consisting of an unstructured string of ASCII characters.

The success of the Internet mail system led to a desire to use it for sending information with a greater degree of structure while staying inside the limits of the character set. A prime example is a document with embedded TROFF formatting commands; a more sophisticated one is a message body encoded in a Page Description Language such as PostScript. In both cases, simply mapping the ASCII characters to the screen or printer in the usual way will not render the document image the sender intended, and an extra processing step is needed to produce it.

Private header fields beginning with X- were already in use by some systems to achieve such a result, for example the Andrew Message System developed at Carnegie Mellon University. The RFC proposes that a new header field, Content-Type, be recognized as the standard field for indicating the structure of the message body, with parameters that specify what structure is used. The memo is explicit that the body would still contain only the ASCII characters allowed by RFC 822, so the proposal should have no impact on existing mailers, only on mail reading systems. That restriction does eliminate more general structuring techniques such as ASN.1 as used in the X.400 messaging standard, which is octet-oriented. This is not the first proposal for structuring message bodies: RFC 767 discusses a proposed technique for structuring multi-media mail messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail bodies were plain ASCII text, with no way to say that the text was really a formatted document. This RFC proposes one header field that names the format, so a reading program can pick the right way to display the message.

sections.title: The Problem of Differing Reader Capabilities
sections.content:
Structured messages raise questions because some receiving systems can process the received message and some cannot, and the RFC asks what to do about the difference.

First, the purpose of structured messages is to send information, ultimately intended for human consumption, that plain ASCII cannot express, such as italics, boldface or Greek characters. Second, insisting on ASCII means a message will not break a reader that cannot process the structure, though the result on the screen may not be readily interpretable. If the sender knows the recipient cannot process PostScript, the sender may prefer to revise the message rather than have it appear incomprehensible, although Greek passages may have no suitable ASCII equivalent.

Ideally the details would be hidden from the sender: the mail system would determine the capabilities of the recipient system and convert the message automatically, or tell the sender it could not be sent. The RFC lists three possible approaches. Each mail system could keep a database of the capabilities of remote systems it knows how to send to, which would be very difficult to keep up to date. Or the mail transport could negotiate with the receiving system and transform the mail into conventional ASCII if the content type is not supported, which would require changes to all existing SMTP implementations and could not be implemented where messages are forwarded over networks that do not implement SMTP. Or an expanded directory service could maintain information on the processing capabilities of receiving hosts, which removes the need for real-time negotiation with the destination but still needs direct interaction with the directory service, and requires changes to existing mailers and a major change to the domain name directory service. The X.400 protocol implements the second approach, and the X.DS directory service recommendations would support the third.

In the interest of facilitating early usage, the RFC recommends none of the three approaches yet, and says a forthcoming RFC will propose a solution based on the second approach. Until then, users would be obliged to keep their own private list of recipient capabilities and to take care not to send PostScript, TROFF or other structured messages to recipients who cannot process them. The penalty is the frustration of a recipient trying to read a raw PostScript or TROFF file painted on the screen. The RFC recognizes that the long-term solution must require changes to mailers, but issues the present RFC in order to begin standardizing the header fields and to facilitate experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some readers can show a formatted message and some cannot, so a sender has to guess. The RFC lists three ways to solve that and then sets the question aside, so that the header field can be agreed first.

sections.title: The Content-Type Header Field
sections.content:
Whatever structuring technique the field names, it must be known precisely to both the sender and the recipient of the message for the message to be properly interpreted. In general this means the allowed parameter values must identify a well-defined, standardized document structuring technique. The RFC does not, however, preclude the use of a parameter value to specify a private structuring technique known only to the sender and the recipient.

The field is proposed to consist of up to four parameter values. The first, the type parameter, names the structuring technique. The second, optional, is a version number, ver-num, which indicates a particular version or revision of the standardized structuring technique. The third is a resource reference, resource-ref, which may indicate a standard database of information to be used in interpreting the structured document. The last is a comment.

In the Extended Backus Naur Form of RFC 822, the RFC gives the field as: Content-Type:= type [";" ver-num [";" 1#resource-ref]] [comment]
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed field has up to four parts: the type of content, a version of that type, a reference to a resource the reader needs, and a free comment. The type comes first and is the only part a reader has to understand.

sections.title: Type Values, Versions and Resource References
sections.content:
The type parameter is initially limited to a set of values, and the values are not case sensitive, so POSTSCRIPT, Postscript and POStscriPT are all equivalent. POSTSCRIPT means the document is encoded in the PostScript Page Definition Language developed by Adobe Systems. SCRIBE means the document contains embedded formatting information in the syntax of the Scribe document formatting language. SGML means the document contains structuring information according to the rules of the Standard Generalized Markup Language, IS 8879, and documents structured according to the ISO DIS 8613 Office Document Architecture and Interchange Format may also be encoded using SGML syntax. TEX means the document contains embedded formatting information in the syntax of the TEX document production language. TROFF means the document contains embedded formatting information in the syntax of the TROFF formatting package. DVI means the document contains information in the device independent file format produced by TROFF or TEX. Any type value beginning with the characters X- is a private value.

Because standard techniques evolve over time, a version number can be given, and the valid values depend on the type parameter. For POSTSCRIPT the values are 1.0, 2.0 and null. For SCRIBE they are 3, 4, 5 and null. For SGML the value is IS.8879.1986 or null.

The resource reference names a well known resource that the receiving system should use when processing the message. The RFC gives the example of a LaserPrep file, which the Macintosh transmits to the Laserwriter to supply font and macro definitions that later documents can call on, which makes those documents considerably more compact than if each had to include the LaserPrep file. Resource references could also name macro packages for use with TEX, or references to preprocessors such as eqn and tbl for use with troff. For POSTSCRIPT the proposed values are laserprep2.9, laserprep3.0, laserprep3.1, laserprep4.0 or a local part. For TROFF they are eqn, tbl, me or a local part. The comment field can be any additional comment text the user desires, enclosed in parentheses as specified in RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists six standard content types, from PostScript to TeX, and allows a private type that starts with X-. Each type can carry a version number and, for some types, the name of a helper file the reader should use.

sections.title: Registration and the Near-Term Use
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that a standardized Content-Type field lets mail reading systems identify the type of a structured message body and process it for display accordingly, while the body still conforms to the RFC 822 requirements concerning allowable characters. A mail reading system need not take any specific action upon receiving a message with a valid Content-Type header field, but recognizing the field and invoking the appropriate display process improves readability and allows the exchange of messages containing mathematical symbols or foreign language characters.

In the near term, the major use of a Content-Type field is likely to be for designating the message body as containing a Page Description Language representation such as PostScript. Additional type values are to be registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Coordinator at USC-ISI.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo expects the field to be used first for page description languages such as PostScript, and asks that any new type be registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Coordinator.
